en: The First Fascicle of the Ritual for Repentance at the Altar of Compassion.
These four characters, "Altar of Compassion" (*Cibei Daochang*), were established due to a dream-vision of Maitreya Bhagavat.
Since his compassion flourishes in this world and his pity reaches into future kalpas, the title was given according to these facts.
I dare not alter or change this name.
By virtue of the power of this mindfulness, I uphold it.
To protect the Triple Gem,
to cause Māra to be obscured,
and to subdue those with great and excessive pride.
Those who have not yet planted roots of goodness shall now be caused to plant them;
those who have already planted roots of goodness...
Now, I cause them to increase.
As for those who calculate that there is something to be attained and abide in various views,
I cause them all to give rise to the mind of renunciation and abandonment.
For those who delight in the lesser Dharma,
cause them to have no doubt regarding the Great Dharma;
for those who delight in the Great Dharma...
It causes joy to arise.
Furthermore, this compassion is the king among all wholesome qualities and the place of refuge for all sentient beings.
Like the sun illuminating the day,
like the moon illuminating the night,
he is the eye for all people.
He is a guide for all people;
he is a parent to all people;
he is a brother to all people.
Together they return to the site of enlightenment as true spiritual friends;
their compassionate kinship is more profound than that of blood and flesh.
They follow one another through successive lifetimes and do not part even in death; therefore,
the eyes and so forth are equal to the mind,
and they are designated as such as stated above.
Today, at this site of practice,
the great assembly of both the hidden and the manifest has established this method of repentance and aroused the Great Mind.
There are twelve great causal conditions.
What are these twelve?
First, the vow to transform the six realms of existence with a mind that has no limit or boundary.
Second, it is to repay the boundless merit of their compassionate kindness.
Third, by the power of this wholesome merit,
may all sentient beings receive the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts and never give rise to the thought of transgression.
Fourth, by this power of merit,
may all sentient beings not give rise to arrogance toward their elders and superiors.
Fifth, by this power of merit...
May all sentient beings, in whatever place they are born, not give rise to thoughts of anger.
Sixth, by the power of this merit,
may all sentient beings not give rise to thoughts of envy toward the physical forms of others.
Seventh, by this power of goodness,
may all sentient beings give rise to no mind of stinginess regarding internal or external phenomena.
Eighth, by this power of goodness...
May all sentient beings, in whatever merit they cultivate, not do so for their own sake,
but entirely for the sake of all those who are unprotected.
Ninth, by this power of goodness...
To cause all sentient beings not to practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for their own sake;
tenth, by the power of this merit,
to cause all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of rescue and relief upon seeing those who are solitary, imprisoned, or afflicted by illness.
May they attain peace and happiness.
Eleventh, by the power of this merit,
if there are sentient beings...
Those who should be subdued, one subdues;
those who should be gathered in, one gathers in.
Twelfth, by means of this power of goodness.
May all sentient beings, in whatever place they are born, always remember and give rise to the bodhicitta,
ensuring that this bodhicitta continues in an uninterrupted succession.
We look up with aspiration to the great assembly of those in the hidden and manifest realms, both ordinary and sagely.
May they equally provide protection and equally provide acceptance,
so that for such-and-such persons— each having called their own name— their confessions shall be purified and their aspirations fulfilled, following this same pattern for all.

Equalizing one's mind with that of all Buddhas and aligning one's vows with those of all Buddhas, may all beings of the six realms and four modes of birth follow along to fulfill the vow for Bodhi. Purify the three karmas through this Dharma: purify the body by bathing; purify the mouth by praising the merits of the Buddha; and purify the mind by directing the heart toward repentance. Once the three karmas are purified, [one attains liberation].
One should then direct the mind toward taking refuge in the Three Jewels, the Great Compassionate Father.

First, taking refuge in the Three Jewels; Second, severing doubt; Third, repentance; Fourth, generating the bodhicitta; Fifth, making vows; Sixth, generating the mind of dedication. 1. Taking Refuge in the Three Jewels (First): To cast oneself entirely upon them is called "refuge" (*śaraṇa*); to rely upon them from beginning to end is called "reliance" (*gati*). Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners in this ritual arena...
Each and every person should give rise to the thought of awakening that the world is impermanent;
that the physical form does not endure for long,
and that youth must inevitably decline.
Do not rely on your physical appearance to dwell in impure conduct.
All things are impermanent and must return to death;
who in heaven or on earth can remain forever?
Though one may be young with a complexion and skin of radiant luster,
and though one’s breath be fragrant and pure— none of these can preserve the body.
In human life, all unions must ultimately return to decay and extinction.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death arrive without a fixed time;
who can eliminate them for my sake?
When calamities suddenly descend, one cannot escape them.
Once all people, whether noble or base, have died because of this,
their bodies swell and emit an unbearable stench;
what benefit is there in cherishing them in vain?
Unless one diligently practices sublime deeds, there is no way to achieve liberation.
We, [Name] and others, reflect upon ourselves:
our forms are like the morning dew, and our lives are as swift as the setting sun.
Born into this world in poverty, I possess no virtue worthy of praise;
my wisdom lacks the sagely brilliance of a divine great being,
and my discernment lacks the penetrating illumination of a sage.
In speech, they lack the beauty of loyalty, harmony, benevolence, and goodness;
in conduct, they lack the propriety of advancing and retreating, or of high and low.
They perversely establish such ambitions, wearying those who are benevolent.
Looking up to you, the great assembly, our hearts are filled with mutual shame and trepidation; now that the date for the Dharma assembly has been set, it is too late to pursue our longing.
From this one parting, I pray that each of you will exert yourselves, diligently applying your minds morning and evening to personally attend upon and make offerings to him.
If people apply themselves with even greater diligence,
this alone will bring true joy.
I pray that the great assembly will each uphold their resolve.
Donning the armor of patience and entering the profound Dharma-gate,
you members of this assembly who share the same practice at this site of enlightenment today should each with earnest gravity arouse a courageous and resolute mind.
With a mind of non-negligence, he abides with a focused mind,
a great mind,
and a superior mind.
A mind of great compassion;
a mind that delights in goodness; a mind of joy.
The mind of repaying kindness;
the mind of delivering all beings;
the mind of protecting all beings.
It protects and saves all minds;
it is identical to the mind of a bodhisattva and equal to the mind of a Tathāgata.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself with the five limbs touching the ground,
and on behalf of the kings, sovereigns, the land and its people, parents, teachers and elders, and those of superior,
middling, and inferior seats— whether they be virtuous or evil associates— [pay homage].
The various devas, rishis, and the Four World-Protecting Kings who reward the good and punish the evil;
the Dragon Kings of the five directions and the eight classes of dragon deities who protect those who uphold mantras;
and, extensively, all sentient beings throughout the ten directions—endless and inexhaustible—who possess spirit and consciousness, whether dwelling in water or on land.
All sentient beings throughout the realm of empty space,
take refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions, as far as the limits of space— one prostration.
Take refuge in all the Honored Dharmas of the ten directions, as far as the limits of space— one prostration.
One prostration to all the worthy and holy ones throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space.
Why must the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this day’s dharma-assembly take refuge in the Triple Gem?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess boundless and impartial great compassion,
by which they deliver and liberate the world.
He possesses boundless, impartial great compassion that brings solace to the world,
regarding all sentient beings as if they were his only child.
With great kindness and great compassion, they are ever free from weariness;
constantly seeking virtuous deeds, they benefit all beings,
vowing to extinguish the fires of the three poisons within sentient beings.
I shall teach and transform sentient beings so that they may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood,
I vow not to realize perfect enlightenment myself.
For this reason, one must take refuge.
Furthermore, the compassion with which the Buddhas regard sentient beings exceeds that of parents.
The Sūtra says:
"The parental affection of parents for their children is limited to a single lifetime;
the compassionate mind of the Buddha toward sentient beings is inexhaustible."
Furthermore, when parents see their child betraying their kindness and violating righteousness, resentment arises in their hearts and their loving-kindness becomes diminished.
The compassionate minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this;
seeing these sentient beings, their compassion becomes even more profound,
such that they enter even into the great wheel of fire within the Avīci Hell.
They undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.
Thus we know that the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas cherish and care for sentient beings more than their own parents do.
Yet all sentient beings, their wisdom shrouded by ignorance and their minds obscured by afflictions,
do not know how to turn toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they neither believe nor accept the Dharma teachings used for their transformation and instruction.
They even resort to coarse speech and engage in slander;
they have never once resolved their minds to contemplate the kindness of the Buddhas,
owing to their lack of faith.
They fall into the various evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
they traverse the three paths of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering until their transgressions are exhausted and they are finally able to escape.
Having been born briefly among humans,
they lack the complete sensory faculties as their own adornment and possess no water of meditative concentration.
Such obstacles as the sword of lack of wisdom arise from a lack of faith;
among all the sins of the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment today,
the sin of disbelief is the gravest of all.
It causes practitioners to be unable to see the Buddha for a long time;
thus, on this day, let each of you feel a sense of urgency and resolve,
humbling your will and tempering your emotions.
Generating a resolute mind and giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse,
they prostrate themselves to seek mercy and repent for their past transgressions.
Once the karmic burdens are exhausted, both the internal and external are purified.
Thereafter, one should direct the visualization into the gate of entrustment.
If one does not give rise to such a mind and direct such an intention,
there is constant fear that [the practice] will be cut off, obstructed, or hindered, making it difficult to penetrate.
Once this direction is lost, one will fall into darkness from which there is no return.
How could one not prostrate oneself with all five limbs like a great mountain collapsing,
single-mindedly taking refuge in faith without further doubt?
We, [Name] and others, today, through the compassionate power of mind of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
have for the first time received awakening and give rise to profound shame and remorse.
We pray that you will grant our request to extinguish the transgressions we have already committed.
I dare not commit again any sins not yet committed.
From this day forth until I reach enlightenment,
I shall give rise to firm faith and never again regress.
We, such-and-such persons, renounce this life and body;
whether we are reborn in the realm of hell-beings or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Whether born into the realm of animals,
the realm of humans,
or the realm of devas.
Within the three realms, whether one receives a male body, a female body,
or a body that is neither male nor female, etc.
Whether great or small, whether ascending or descending,
and though subjected to various oppressions and afflictions that are difficult to endure or bear,
I vow not to let my faith of this day be lost or diminished on account of suffering.
I would rather undergo all manner of sufferings for a thousand or ten thousand kalpas than,
on account of such suffering, ever retreat from or lose the faith I hold today.
I look up with aspiration to all Buddhas, the Great Earth, and the Bodhisattvas.
May they equally provide protection and equally provide guidance,
causing such-and-such individuals to have firm resolve in faith and to become equal to the minds of all Buddhas.
They share the vows of all Buddhas;
they cannot be destroyed by any demons or non-Buddhists.
Together, they direct their sincere minds with equal and profound earnestness.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground,
one bows once in refuge to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space;
one bows once in refuge to all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space.
One prostration in taking refuge in all the worthy and holy ones throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space.
Today, you members of this assembly sharing the same practice at this site of enlightenment,
listen well with minds properly composed.
The world of humans and devas is illusory and deceptive;
because this illusion is not real, there is no substantial fruit.
Being false, hollow, and fragile, it undergoes endless change and transformation.
Because there is no real fruit,
one remains long stalled in the stream of birth and death;
because of constant transition and change.
For this reason, they long drift upon the ocean of suffering through pervasive attachment.
Such sentient beings are objects of the noble ones' compassionate concern.
Thus, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
When Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood, each has their own original vow;
Śākyamuni did not manifest a long life,
but instead shortened it to a brief span.
Compassionate toward these sentient beings who have suddenly fallen into the ocean of suffering and cannot escape it,
he remains in this land to rescue those who are wicked and depraved; thus,
his teachings contain words that are stern, forceful, and harsh.
Without abandoning suffering, one delivers sentient beings;
never without the mind that extensively rescues and benefits them through the skillful means of wholesome dharmas.
Thus, the Samādhi Sūtra says:
The mind of all Buddhas is great compassion;
that which is the object of this compassion is suffering sentient beings.
When he sees sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction,
it is as if an arrow has pierced his heart,
or as if his own eyes have been torn out.
Having seen this, he wept with grief, finding no moment of peace in his heart;
desiring to uproot their suffering and grant them peace and happiness,
he reflected that the wisdom of all Buddhas is equal and their transformations are uniform.
As for Śākyamuni being specifically praised as "valiant," it is because he was able to endure suffering to deliver sentient beings;
one should know that the compassionate grace of our Original Teacher is truly profound.
Amongst suffering and afflicted sentient beings,
you are able to speak various words to benefit them all;
yet today we have not received liberation.
Advancing, I did not hear the purport of a single sound;
retreating, I did not behold the hidden splendor beneath the twin trees.
This was truly because my karmic obstructions separated my thoughts from compassion.
From this day forward, let us together give rise to a mind of sorrowful longing;
because we long for the Tathāgata with such sorrowful longing,
our wholesome minds will become profound and intense.
Already immersed in suffering, they recalled the grace of the Tathāgata;
sobbing and tormented with remorse, their faces flushed with shame and their voices choked with grief,
they were moved by a single, piercing pain and prostrated themselves, casting their five limbs to the ground.
With a sincere heart, I respectfully dedicate this for the sake of kings,
sovereigns, the land and its people, parents, teachers and elders, donors who provide offerings, virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends,
and all devas and rishis who are intelligent and upright.
The heavens and earth, the void, the Four Heavenly Kings who protect the world—who reward the good and punish the evil—and those who guard and uphold the dhāraṇī;
the Dragon Kings of the five directions, the dragon deities, and the eight classes of beings;
extending broadly to all infinite and inexhaustible sentient beings throughout the ten directions, [I take refuge] again and again.
One prostration in taking refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
One prostration in taking refuge in all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
One prostration to all the worthy and holy ones throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space.
Together, with sincere resolve, kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, one recites these words aloud:
"Thus it is said."
The Buddhas, the Great Holy Ones, have awakened to all phenomena without exception;
they are the unsurpassed teachers of gods and humans. Therefore, they are the refuge.
All dharmas are eternally abiding; this is the pure Sūtra.
Because they can eliminate the diseases of body and mind,
the Bodhisattvas of the great earth are my refuge; because they are free from attachment and the four types of śramaṇas can rescue all from suffering, they are my refuge.
The Triple Gem protects the world; I now prostrate with my head at their feet.
To all beings within the six realms, I now take refuge entirely.
May their compassion cover all, causing everyone to attain peace and happiness.
"Those who have compassion for sentient beings— We all together take refuge,
prostrating ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground.
Each of us thinks to ourselves:"
I look up with aspiration to all the Triple Gem of the ten directions:

by the power of compassion, the power of original vows, the power of great spiritual penetrations, the inconceivable power, the power of immeasurable mastery, the power to liberate sentient beings, the power to protect and shelter sentient beings, and the power to comfort sentient beings.
May all sentient beings fully awaken and understand that [Name] and others today take refuge in the Triple Gem;
by the power of this merit, may they attain [their goal].
May all sentient beings each obtain their respective wishes.
For those among the devas and ṛṣis,
may they exhaust all outflows (āsravas).
If they are among the asuras, they abandon the habit of arrogance;
if they are in the human realm, they no longer experience manifold sufferings;
and if they are in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
They shall immediately be liberated and freed from it.
Furthermore, today, whether they hear the names of the Triple Gem or not,
by the spiritual power of the Buddha, [they shall be saved].
May all sentient beings attain complete liberation and ultimately achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
May they together with all bodhisattvas ascend to perfect enlightenment with a single prostration.

2. Severing Doubt, Part Two. Because all sentient beings have not yet abandoned doubt and confusion, they give rise to many obstacles regarding the Dharma; therefore, it is now necessary to sever this doubt forever. Today, at this site of enlightenment, the great assembly of fellow practitioners—
Listen attentively with a single mind.
Now, the principle that causes and effects, influences and responses,
and mutual inductions arise one from another is an inevitable truth, free from any discrepancy.
Yet the karmic actions of sentient beings are not uniform;
good and evil alternate.
Because their karma is not uniform, [the results vary].
Because retribution involves degrees of refinement or coarseness—
whether noble or base, good or evil—
the manifestations thereof are not uniform, but differ in myriad ways.
Since there are already discrepancies and one does not understand one's fundamental practice,
because of this lack of understanding, doubts and delusions arise in confusion. Some say:
One who diligently upholds the precepts ought to attain longevity,
yet one sees those with short lifespans;
a butcher ought to meet an early end, yet one sees him live long.
Yet, on the contrary, their lifespans are extended;
those of upright integrity and purity ought to be summoned by abundance,
yet they are seen to suffer in poverty and hardship.
A person who covets and steals ought to encounter misfortune and ruin;
yet they instead enjoy abundance.
Who among those who harbor such doubts would not feel resentment?
Yet they do not know that this is brought about by the causes planted through past karma.
Furthermore, as clarified in the Prajñā[pāramitā],
if there are those who read and recite this sutra...
Those who are despised and treated with contempt by others were destined for the evil realms due to the karmic offenses of their previous lives;
it is because of these [past deeds] that they are now despised by people in this world.
The sinful karma of previous lives will then be extinguished.
As for why sentient beings are unable to have deep faith in the words of the sutras and harbor such doubts,
it is entirely due to the delusions of ignorance.
They give rise to deluded inversions;
furthermore, they do not believe that that which is within the three realms is suffering, nor do they believe that that which is outside the three realms is bliss.
Whenever they are defiled by worldly things, they all claim it to be bliss.
If one says that it is pleasant,
why does the sensation of suffering arise within it?
For example, excessive food and drink result in illness.
The breath is labored and gasping, and the body is distended with piercing pain.
Furthermore, when one reaches for clothing, one sees only further distress and toil.
When one obtains fine silks and linens in the cold, the sense of gratitude becomes thin and mindfulness shallow.
When one who is suffering from heat sees heavy furs, their distress is already profound;
if these were truly pleasure, why would such distress arise?
Therefore, we know that food, drink, and clothing are truly not pleasure.
Furthermore, as for the claim that one finds joy in one's kin,
then one ought to remain in perpetual delight, with singing and laughter without end;
why then do they suddenly become subject to impermanence and vanish so abruptly?
What was present just now is gone; what existed just now has perished.
One cries out to heaven and strikes the earth, with the liver and heart broken into pieces.
Furthermore, one knows not whence life comes nor whither death goes.
Cherishing their grief, they see each other off as far as the most remote mountains;
grasping hands in a final parting, they bid farewell for ten thousand kalpas.
For those who experience such things, the suffering is immeasurable.
Sentient beings, through deluded views, claim that [this] is pleasure;
yet they all say that the causes of supramundane happiness are suffering.
Or they see [the practice of] advancing to eat coarse vegetables, mortifying the body, and eating at fixed times.
They abandon light and soft garments to practice wearing rag-robes from refuse heaps,
all claiming that such things are a matter of forcing oneself to undergo hardship;
they do not realize that this practice is the path to liberation.

Or they may see those who practice giving, upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, walking meditation, prostration, and recitation—people who are tireless and persevering—and yet all say that these are suffering;
they do not realize that such practices cultivate the mind that transcends the world.
If there comes a day of illness or death,
one immediately gives rise to doubt,
spending the entire day exhausting both mind and body.
There is not a moment’s rest.
How can human strength endure this?
If one does not exert oneself diligently, how could one avoid falling into exhaustion?
To pointlessly lose one's body and life serves no purpose;
yet some maintain their own doctrines, which are indeed true to reality,
without knowing how to trace back from effects to causes.
One falsely constructs these delusions;
if one encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), those delusions may be eliminated,
but if one encounters an evil friend (pāpamitra), one's ignorance becomes even more profound.
Because of doubt and confusion, one falls into the three evil realms;
once within those evil realms, what can regret accomplish?
O great assembly of fellow practitioners at this day’s site of enlightenment!
The causes and conditions for such doubts are immeasurable;
moreover, even beyond the three realms, the habitual tendencies of doubt have not yet been exhausted.
How much more so now, when this present form cannot suddenly depart;
this life is not severed, but rather increases further,
and we, the great assembly, must together traverse a long journey ahead.
Practice asceticism yourself;
you should rely on the Buddha’s words and practice according to the teachings,
without harboring doubts or excusing yourself through weariness.
The reason why the Buddhas and noble sages are able to transcend birth and death and reach the other shore is truly due to the merit accumulated through the practice of goodness;
thus they attain unimpeded, sovereign liberation.
We have not yet escaped birth and death today;
we ourselves are already pitiable.
How can we allow ourselves to remain greedily dwelling in this evil world?
Now, fortunately, my four elements have not yet declined;
the five blessings are peaceful and sound.
My movements and activities, my coming and going, are all as I desire.
If you do not exert effort now, what more can you wait for?
In the past life, you already failed to see the Truth;
in this present life, you are wasting it away again without attaining any realization.
As for how we shall deliver them in future ages,
I press my chest and contemplate my heart with a truly sorrowful disposition.
The great assembly today should only exhort one another to strive and practice diligently.
One must not say again, "Let us wait and see;
the Path of the Sages is long and vast, difficult to accomplish in a single day.
Thus, one day passes, and then another day follows.
When shall I attain the state where what was to be done has been accomplished?
Now, perhaps due to reciting sutras, practicing seated meditation, or diligently performing ascetic practices,
I have fallen slightly ill.
He then said, "This is the result of my diligent and arduous recitation and study," yet he did not realize that had he not performed these practices,
he would have died long ago.
It is because of practicing this path that we have reached the present day.
Furthermore, the increase and decrease of the four great elements resulting in disease are constant;
even up to old age and death, they cannot be avoided.
Life in this world inevitably leads to decay and extinction.
If you wish to attain the Way, you must rely on the Buddha’s words;
to do otherwise and yet achieve it is impossible.
This is impossible.
Because all sentient beings have contravened the Buddha’s words,
they transmigrate through the three miserable realms and undergo every kind of suffering.
If it is as the Buddha has said— that there is no respite at all and one must be diligent in all dharmas as if one's head were on fire—
do not let this life pass without attainment.
Let each and every person among us feel this with equal and profound urgency.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground like a great mountain collapsing,
I pay homage on behalf of my conscious spirits from the past until this present life,
and for my parents throughout successive births.
Throughout kalpas of successive lifetimes, they have been one's close kin:
the Preceptor (Upādhyāya), the Ācārya,
the honored witnesses from the same ordination platform, and the senior, middle, and junior seats.
Faithful donors, both virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends,
the various devas and ṛṣis, and the four world-protecting kings who reward the good and punish the evil.
May the mantra-holders be protected by the dragon kings of the five directions, the nāgas, and the eight classes of beings,
extending widely to all infinite and inexhaustible sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
I take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

Homage to Maitreya Buddha; homage to Vipaśyin Buddha; homage to Śikhin Buddha; homage to Viśvabhū Buddha; homage to Krakucchanda Buddha; homage to Kanakamuni Buddha; homage to Kāśyapa Buddha; homage to Śākyamuni Buddha; homage to Anantabuddhakāya Bodhisattva; homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, I take refuge in all the Three Jewels throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space.
May you, through the power of your compassion,
together grant me your protective acceptance.
By means of their supernormal powers, they shall protect, sustain, and receive [beings],
from this day forth until the attainment of Bodhi,
through the four immeasurable minds.
The six pāramitās are constantly manifested before them,
as are the four types of unimpeded knowledge.
Possessing the power of the six supernormal knowledges and mastery over the mind,
they practice the bodhisattva path and enter the wisdom of the Buddha.
With one prostration, may all beings throughout the ten directions together ascend to perfect enlightenment.
Today, you members of this assembly who share the same karmic affinity at this site of practice,
once again with sincere resolve, skillfully gather and focus your minds and thoughts.
Since we have already entered the gate of faith and devotion,
we should simply maintain our resolve and take the onward course as our goal;
let there be no further hindrance regarding internal or external phenomena.
If one's fundamental karma is not clear,
one cannot create [merit] by oneself;
when seeing others performing meritorious deeds, one should only encourage and exhort them.
By snapping the fingers and joining the palms, one should manifest the advancement of their virtue;
it is not fitting to give rise to thoughts that create obstacles, causing the mind of that practitioner to become hindered or retreat.
If they do not retreat, their progress shall continue as before.
Since there is no decrease for them, you will only harm yourself;
what benefit is there to your body in vainly fabricating right and wrong?
If one can remain unimpeded regarding what is wholesome, [one will not suffer].
He may be called a great person of power who accords with the Way.
If he were to create obstacles now,
how could he possibly attain penetration into the Buddha-way in future lives?
When investigated according to principle, the actual gravity of the harm is profound;
the sin of obstructing another's roots of goodness is truly not slight.
As stated in the *Mukha-rakṣa-sūtra*:
There was a hungry ghost whose form was so hideous that those who saw it had their hair stand on end and were filled with dread.
Their bodies emit fierce flames like a mass of fire;
their mouths produce an endless stream of maggots;
and they adorn themselves with pus, blood, and various decaying impurities.
The stench permeates far and wide, making it impossible to draw near.
Sometimes flames issue from their mouths and fire erupts from their limbs;
they wail aloud and run hither and thither.
At that time, the Arhat Pūrṇa asked the hungry ghost,
"What sin did you commit in your past life that you now undergo this suffering?
The hungry ghost replied:
In the past, when I was a śramaṇa,
I was attached to the necessities of life;
being stingy with food, I could not relinquish it.
They do not maintain dignified deportment;
their speech is coarse and evil.

4. Generating the Bodhicitta. Fourth, regarding the generation of the bodhicitta:
today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice have together succeeded in washing away the defilements of their minds;
the grave obstacles of the ten non-virtues are purified and exhausted without remainder.
Once the accumulation of karma has been dispelled and both the internal and external are purified,
one should next look up to and emulate the Bodhisattvas’ practice of the direct path;

for it is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) capable of accomplishing all tasks.
I pray that each member of the great assembly shall firm their resolve.
Do not wait for the exhaustion of your allotted lifespan;
do not let it pass in vain,
lest you later regret it to no avail.
We have met this auspicious time together today;
you should not allow afflictions to cloud your minds day and night.
You ought to exert yourselves and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
The bodhicitta is itself the Buddha-mind;
its merit and wisdom are beyond measure.
This is already true for a single thought-moment, let alone many.
Even if one were to cultivate immeasurable merit throughout successive kalpas,
and even if one were to fully practice all other virtues in this present life,
it would not equal even a ten-thousandth part of the merit of generating the bodhicitta.
Even calculations and metaphors cannot fully exhaust [the extent of this].
Furthermore, there is another person who performs only meritorious deeds.
If one does not give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta,
it is like plowing a field without sowing seeds;
since there is no sprout, where can one seek the fruit?
For this reason, one must resolve to generate the bodhicitta as a causal condition for realization;
thus, above, one repays the Buddha's kindness, and below, one uproots all suffering.
Therefore, the Buddha praised the sons of the gods, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said."
To generate the bodhicitta for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings is the foremost offering to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the arousal of the bodhicitta is not to be done only once;
rather, it should be aroused repeatedly so that the continuity of the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One has made great and virtuous vows in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers.

Furthermore, regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta:
it may arise simply upon encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
it does not necessarily require meeting a Buddha appearing in the world.
Just as when Mañjuśrī first turned toward Bodhi,
it was through a woman that he gave rise to his initial resolve;

there is no distinction between enemies and kin, and the six realms of existence are of one single aspect.
May all, by virtue of this merit, attain liberation together.
If you share this same faith and understanding, know that this is not mere conceptual proliferation.
Today, at this site of enlightenment, for the great assembly of those with common karma:
When generating the bodhicitta,
one must first give rise to the thought of focusing on those with whom one has an intimate connection; that is,
one should bring to mind one's own parents, teachers, elders, and kinsmen.
Furthermore, he recollects the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals;
he recollects all the devas, the rishis, and all the benevolent deities;
and he recollects all human beings in the human realm.
When there are those who suffer, how should one rescue them?
Having seen them, one should give rise to this thought:
"Only a great mind can extract them from their suffering."
If the perception of one is accomplished, one should form the perception of two;
once the perception of two is accomplished, one should form the perception of three;
once the perception of three is accomplished, one should form the perception of filling an entire room.
Once the single room was filled, it extended to fill one *yojana*;
once the *yojana* was filled, it filled Jambudvīpa;
once Jambudvīpa was filled, it filled the three continents.
In this way, it gradually expanded to fill the worlds of the ten directions.
He saw that all sentient beings in the eastern direction were none other than his own father.
All sentient beings of the western direction have been her mothers;
all sentient beings of the southern direction have been her elder brothers;
and all sentient beings of the northern direction have been her younger brothers.
"All sentient beings below are my sisters;
all sentient beings above are my teachers and elders;
and all others in the four intermediate directions are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. Having seen this, he formed this thought.
If, when experiencing suffering, one conceives the thought of a self,
one should go to those people, massage their bodies, and vow to uproot their suffering.
Once they have attained liberation, one should preach the Dharma for them.
They praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Having offered these praises, their hearts were filled with joy;
they perceived his experience of bliss as no different from their own, just like the great assembly of fellow practitioners at the site of enlightenment today.
Having resolved upon bodhicitta,
one should act in this way: not abandoning suffering while delivering sentient beings,
for their mutual pain is equal to one's own.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, they should contemplate in their hearts and speak with their mouths,
making this vow: "We, [Name] and others,
from this day forth until we reach the site of enlightenment..."
Throughout that interval, in whatever place they are born,
may they encounter virtuous spiritual friends and constantly give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta.
If one is in the three miserable realms or has fallen into the eight difficult conditions,
may they always be made to remember and give rise to the bodhicitta,
so that the succession of the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted for even a single prostration.
Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice should arouse a courageous mind and make a solemn vow to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
With equal intensity and sincerity, prostrate yourselves with your five limbs touching the ground and take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

from this moment until we reach the site of enlightenment.
One vows not to retreat while practicing the bodhisattva path;
one constantly maintains the mind to deliver sentient beings and constantly maintains the mind to establish sentient beings in liberation.
He constantly maintains a mind that protects and shelters all sentient beings,
vowing not to attain perfect enlightenment before all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood.

all Bodhisattvas of the great earth, and all worthy sages will appear to bear witness for me.

Today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of enlightenment,
even if they have practiced many kinds of goodness throughout kalpas, [may they likewise attain fulfillment].
Thus, one may obtain the provisional, flowery rewards of humans and devas,
yet fails to attain the ultimate, supramundane fruits;
when their lifespan ends and their merit is exhausted, they fall back into the evil realms.
When the body perishes and is oppressed by suffering, one cannot escape it on one's own.
Unless one establishes great vows and gives rise to the vast mind,
there is no way to forever leave behind the decay and afflictions of birth and death.
Together today, we should only focus our minds on the Buddhas,
give rise to firm resolve, and awaken the bodhicitta.
The merit of awakening this mind is beyond measure.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas could not exhaustively describe it;
such wholesome power is inconceivable.
How could one fail to study it with a sincere heart and single-minded devotion?
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"For example, a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a room that has been dark for a hundred years.
Do not say that a single thought-moment of mind is insignificant and thus fail to exert yourself."
Together, kneel with one mind,
join your palms, and direct your attention universally toward all the Triple Gem in the ten directions,

We, [Name] and others, now, before all Buddhas of the ten directions,
before all Honored Dharmas of the ten directions,
and before all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Before all the worthy ones and holy sages of the ten directions,
kneel on your right knee with palms joined, and with a straightforward mind, right mindfulness, a heart of profound reverence,
and a mind free from negligence.
The mind abiding in tranquility,
the mind delighting in goodness,
and the mind that transcends all.
Protecting all minds,
equalizing them with the mind of all Buddhas,
one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
From this day forth until we reach the seat of enlightenment, we, [Name] and others,
shall not give rise to the mind of a human or a deva,
nor shall we give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka.
They do not give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha,
but only give rise to the Mahāyāna mind—
the mind that seeks all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and achieves anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I only pray that all Buddhas, great earth Bodhisattvas, and all holy beings throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space,
by the power of their original vows, will manifest before me as witnesses.
Through the power of compassion, may they be assisted and sustained,
so that such-and-such persons, having today resolved their minds, shall remain firm and non-regressive in whatever place of birth they are born;
even if they should fall into the three miserable realms or encounter the eight difficulties.
Within the three realms, they undergo various bodies and experience various sufferings that are difficult to endure and hard to bear.
I vow that I shall not, on account of suffering, retreat from or lose this great resolve of today;
rather, I would prefer to enter the great wheel of fire in the Avīci Hell and undergo all manner of sufferings.
I vow not to allow myself to be discouraged by suffering,
nor to fall away from the great resolve of this day;
for this mind and this vow are equal to the minds of all Buddhas.
In accordance with the vows of all Buddhas,
we once again most sincerely prostrate before the Triple Gem.
From this moment until we attain Buddhahood, [we, such-and-such persons, etc.]...
Not abandoning these two dharmas:
knowing that all dharmas are empty,
yet not abandoning any sentient beings.
Together, with single-minded sincerity and equal, piercing earnestness,
prostrate yourselves with your five limbs touching the ground, and with mind and mouth recite:
"We, such-and-such persons, do not seek unsurpassed bodhi for our own sake."
For the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings,
I shall attain unsurpassed bodhi;
from this moment until the attainment of Buddhahood.
I vow to shoulder the burden of all infinite and boundless sentient beings,
giving rise to great compassion until the end of the future;
should any sentient being have heavy offenses leading to the three miserable realms or suffer hardships within the six destinies, [I shall deliver them].
We, [Name] and others, vow not to avoid any suffering,
but to protect with our own bodies so that these sentient beings may attain a state of peace and security;
we rely solely upon all the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space.

One ghost asked:

Furthermore, there was another ghost.

Do not act out of season;
wait until the guests have departed before proceeding with the usual residence.

"You gave rise to a thieving mind and struck [the vessel] to take a small amount.

the ultimate fruit lies in hell.

Departing from Hell, Departing from Hell, Part Two. Having already fully described the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions—how one falls into the evil realms due to unwholesome karma—I shall now once again manifest the gates of hell for the assembly of those with common karma at this present site of enlightenment.
Although the myriad phenomena differ in category and their functions are not uniform,
when it comes to the contrast between light and darkness,
there is only good and evil.
To speak of the good results in the superior realms of humans and devas;
to describe the evil results in the three miserable paths—
these two matters are clearly manifest in the world and are not false.
Yet those who are foolish and deluded frequently give rise to doubts and dissent;
some claim that humans and devas are falsely constructed,
and that the hells are not a true teaching.
They do not know how to infer the cause by examining the effect,
nor do they know how to seek the cause by examining the effect.
Since they fail to distinguish between cause and effect, [they remain deluded].
Each adheres to their own worldly interpretations;
they do not merely speak of emptiness,
but even when discussing existence, they compose titles for works and write treatises.
Their minds are alienated from supreme goodness and they have never uttered a word of error;
even when shown instruction, their attachments remain stubbornly firm.
Such people as these cast themselves into the evil realms.
In the time it takes to shoot an arrow, one falls into hell.
Neither a compassionate parent nor a filial child can save one;
one can only proceed forward into the fiery cauldrons.
Body and mind are shattered, and the spirit suffers in agony;
at such a time, what avail would repentance be?
O great assembly of fellow practitioners in this day’s dharma-assembly!
Good and evil assist one another like shadows and echoes;
sins and blessings follow their respective places, prepared and maintained from long before.

What is meant by "hell"?
The Sūtra states that the region between the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) within the trichiliocosm,
where there is darkness, is called hell.
The iron city is one hundred and sixty million li in length and breadth.
Within the city are eighty-four thousand partitions; below they have iron for their ground, and above they have iron for their nets.
Fire burns this city until its interior and exterior are glowing red;
the fire from above penetrates below, and the fire from below penetrates above.
Its names include the Crushing Hell, the Hell of Darkness, the Hell of the Wheel of Blades, and the Forest of Swords.
The forest of iron spikes,
the iron nets and iron caves,

Charcoal pits burning forests;

The fiery chariots and flaming wheels;

extreme heat and extreme cold.

with iron hooks and iron beaks;

The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Why is it called the Avīci Hell? 'A' means 'non-'"
"Bi" means to obstruct;
"a" means non-existence;
"bi" means to save.
Taken together, they signify "unobstructed" and "without recourse.
Furthermore, *a* means "uninterrupted," and *nā* means "unmoving."
"Ā" signifies extreme heat;
"ni" signifies extreme affliction;
"ā" signifies lack of skill.
The nose says it does not abide.
Not abiding in the unskilled is called Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, "A" signifies a great flame.
The nose says it is "fierce heat.
When fierce fire enters the heart, it is called the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
The Avīci Hell is thirty-two thousand li in length and breadth, exactly equal.
It consists of seven layers of iron walls and seven tiers of iron nets,
with eighteen compartments below.
Surrounding these sevenfold layers are sword-forests.
Within these sevenfold walls, there is further a forest of swords,
consisting of eighteen tiers below.
The cauldron has eighty-four thousand tiers.
At its four corners are four great bronze dogs,
their bodies measuring sixteen thousand li in length.
His eyes are like flashes of lightning;
his fangs are like sword-trees;

His mouth is like the mouth of a yakṣa;

It is said that speech is the medium for expressing virtue and the path for traversing the Way; discourse is the stairway to principle and the guide to sagehood.
Thus, it is by relying on speech that principle becomes manifest.
Because it is principle, it is not mere words;
because it is principle, it is manifested through words, yet words do not transcend principle.
Although words and principle appear to diverge, and good and evil seem utterly distinct, [they are ultimately one].
Nevertheless, the influence and its response correspond without ever being confused or overlapping.
For those at the beginning of their studies,
it is essential to use concise words to realize the Way.
As for those who have attained the state beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*),
they accord with the principle and forget words;
reflecting upon myself, I am but an ordinary fool.
Obscured by heavy delusion,
one has not yet been able to relinquish verbal expressions regarding the various dharma-gates;
because consciousness is now coarse, its subtlety is not fully realized.
Because their insight is shallow, they do not reach its ultimate limit.
Yet, while speaking of it is easy, practicing it is truly difficult;
only sages with sages can fully accomplish it all.
Now there is a challenge: "If you cannot rectify yourself, how can you rectify others?
Your own three karmas are defiled and turbid;
how can you exhort others toward purity?"
It is impossible for one who is themselves impure to desire that others become pure.
Since it is not firm, why urge others toward it?
Now, to speak of emptiness while acting otherwise will surely cause distress to others;
since they have become distressed, why not simply desist?
Reflecting upon this again and again, how could I not feel ashamed?
It was because you are a *kalyāṇamitra* that I spoke these words.
Thereupon, he adjusted his robes, composed his countenance, and remained silent without reply.
Now, hearing these words from the spiritual friend,
my heart is filled with shame and remorse;
I recognize my own profound transgressions.
I did not dare to deceive or mislead the Sage by concealing his errors;
now, fearing that someone might [misunderstand] were I to destroy them, I have preserved them.
Therefore, his merit increased.
Just as he wished to preserve it,
he again feared that someone might harbor slanderous views toward it.
He was at a loss for what to do, vacillating between advancing and retreating; yet,
as the mind that stands in the midst of the repentance rite is already virtuous,
and virtuous dharmas are unimpeded, he should simply exert himself.
One must not calculate this.
Now, relying solely upon the Great Compassionate Father of the world,

if it does not accord with the minds of the assembly, [it will fail].

do not become an evil friend,
but remain a kinsman to enlightenment.

First: Offering Worship to the Buddha for the Realm of Heavenly Beings, Part Two of the Six Realms of Worship to the Buddha. First: Offering Worship to the Buddha for the Realm of Heavenly Beings. Today, at this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the great assembly of fellow practitioners.
The various devas, rishis, and all benevolent deities possess immeasurable and inconceivable grace and virtue toward all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings be ever secure in peace and happiness.
May they diligently protect themselves and follow only what is wholesome.
How is this known? It is because of the Buddha’s injunction.

The Four Heavenly Kings, beginning with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, shall protect with a compassionate heart those who uphold this sutra and hear the name of its compassionate title; just as the Dharma-ministers of the Son of Heaven provide protection,
they further command the sea dragon Īpala to protect with a compassionate heart those who uphold this sutra.
Like one who guards their eyes or loves their own child, they shall not depart for six periods of the day and night;
furthermore, they shall command the yakṣa sons of Yama, as well as countless male and female nāgas,
to protect with a compassionate heart those who uphold this sutra, just as one protects the crown of the head, never daring to touch it.
Furthermore, he commanded King Virūḍhaka:
"With a heart of compassion, protect those who uphold this sutra, never wearying, like a mother’s love for her child; protect them day and night, whether they are walking or standing still.
He also commanded Nanda, Upananda, Sāgara, and Upendra.
With a heart of loving-kindness, they protect those who uphold this sutra;
They revere, make offerings to, and prostrate at their feet, Just as the devas serve Śakra, Or as a filial son honors his parents.
At the site of the Way of Compassion, they bestow peace and happiness, Teaching all sentient beings to form bonds of Dharma-kinship.
In future lives they shall be born before the Buddhas and enter samādhi; Ultimately, they shall attain the stage of non-retrogression.

Those who hear the names of the various Buddhas, And further hear of Avalokiteśvara of Boundless Compassion, Will have the three obstructions eliminated and all evils removed; Endowed with the five eyes, they shall achieve Bodhi.

May all the celestial kings keep everyone in mind and constantly provide encouragement and support with their majestic spiritual power to the assembly of fellow practitioners at today’s site of enlightenment.
May all the celestial kings...
Possessing such benevolence and virtue,
he protects and shelters all sentient beings;
yet these sentient beings—
I have never yet resolved to repay such kindness and virtue;
yet even the ancients were moved by the favor of a single meal to sacrifice their lives and abandon their bodies.
How much more so for the various devas, benevolent spirits, and the eight classes of divine generals,
who possess such kindness and virtue toward all sentient beings.
This kindness and this virtue are of boundless merit;
today we repent and resolve our minds [to follow the path].
All of this is due to the Celestial King’s secret application of supernatural power to assist the practitioner and bring their mind to fulfillment;
were such assistance not bestowed, these states of mind would not be realized.
One would have long since fallen away;
this is why Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas always praise the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
This is a great cause and condition that enables us to ascend to and tread upon the site of enlightenment;
were it not for the spiritual friend, this would not be possible.
How may I come to behold all the Buddhas?
To cast myself down would not suffice to repay their vast benevolence;
to lose my life would not suffice to repay their profound grace.
If even Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas speak such words,
how much more so those below them who would not fail to offer a response?
Today, this great assembly has been unable to sacrifice their bodies or give up their lives.
Therefore, you should for now apply yourselves with diligent effort;
such vigor is also a gradual way of repaying their kindness.
Each of you should strive to further expand your resolve, recognizing and repaying this debt of gratitude.
One must not follow the current;
rather, one should turn back without fixed direction,
rejoicing as before at the great difficulty of having encountered [the teaching] once again.
This present fruit is difficult to obtain;
what more do you wish to wait for?
To lose this single assembly—what a tragedy!
Knowing what further course can be taken,
one should only be courageous and selfless for the sake of others.
Success may be followed by failure, just as spring is followed by winter.
Time does not wait for man;
how could life endure long?
Reflecting on this single parting.
We have no set time for our next meeting;
may each of you exert yourselves.

3. Prostrating to the Buddha on Behalf of One’s Parents. Third: Today, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this site of practice must further prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground on behalf of their parents, in gratitude for the kindness of their upbringing and nourishment.
Cradling them with maternal love and profound affection,
he would rather endanger his own life than fail to establish his children in safety;
once they had grown to maturity, he instructed them in benevolence and propriety.
Washing his hands, he sought a teacher, vowing to master the meaning of the scriptures;
never for a moment did he forget his aspiration to reach the level of the sages.
Whatever was required for his support, he provided without begrudging even his family's treasures.
The knots of anxious thought and recollection have become an illness;
he lies restless upon his mat, constantly remembering his son.
In all the world, such profound parental affection is truly without equal.
Therefore, the Buddha said:

Now, one who has not left the household life cannot yet attain the Way."

where they shall, along with all the bodhisattvas, achieve perfect awakening.

Eighth: Making Vows for the Six Realms. May those of us, such-and-such, by virtue of the merit and causal conditions of this present act of bowing to the Buddha on behalf of the various devas, rishis, nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings, [make these vows].
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space,
across the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, until the end of the future— may they,
from this day forth until they attain Bodhi, [be so].
No longer shall they again unjustly harm their physical bodies;
though they may undergo various forms of suffering and agony, they shall no longer commit the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes.
By virtue of the causal conditions of the merit from their present practice of bowing to the Buddha, they shall withdraw from the three miserable realms.
Each attained the purification of the physical and verbal karma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
each attained all the various mental states of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, including the great earth-like mind.
Giving rise to all roots of goodness;
possessing the ocean-like mind that upholds the great Dharma of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The heart of Mount Sumeru;
the maṇi-jewel heart that causes all to abide securely in unsurpassed bodhi;
the vajra heart that is far removed from afflictions.
With a resolute mind regarding all phenomena that is firm and steadfast,
one cannot be thwarted or destroyed by any māras or non-Buddhists.
With a lotus-like mind, one cannot be defiled by any worldly dharmas.
The pure sun-like mind eliminates all cataracts of ignorance and obscuration.
The empty mind cannot be measured by any sentient beings.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings of the four modes of birth and the six realms [attain this].
From this day forward, contemplate the nature of consciousness and resolve with certainty upon the nature of faith and understanding.
Abandon all frivolity and constantly reflect upon the Dharma.
Give away everything you possess, with a heart free from attachment or stinginess.
With a mind courageous and unyielding, never succumbing to cowardice,
one bestows all cultivated merits upon all beings without returning to the paths of error,
remaining single-mindedly and exclusively focused.
Viewing the good as an illusion and the evil as a dream,
one abandons birth and death and swiftly emerges from the triple world.
Clearly and profoundly observing the most subtle and wondrous Dharma,
each attains the opportunity to make offerings to all Buddhas,
with every requisite for worship being fully provided.
Each attained the opportunity to make offerings to all the Honored Ones of the Dharma;
the requisites for making these offerings were entirely complete.
Each also attained the opportunity to make offerings to all Bodhisattvas.
The various requisites for making offerings were all fully provided;
each was able to offer to all the worthy and holy ones,
and the requisites for offering were entirely complete.
If there are any sentient beings of future generations who,
like so-and-so and others, aspire to the realm of vows this day,
may they all enter the great ocean of vows.
One immediately attains the accomplishment of merit and wisdom;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, one gains mastery according to one's will,
and with a single prostration, one becomes fully enlightened together with the Tathāgata.
Be mindful of impermanence; be mindful of impermanence! Today, in this Dharma assembly, we, the fellow practitioners, have together completed the ritual of repentance for the six realms of existence.
Next, we must further awaken to the reality of impermanence.
Now, the causes and effects of sin and merit across the three periods of time arise in mutual succession;
this resonates deeply within the heart, such that no thought can intervene between them.
One should always consider that cause and effect correspond as surely as a shadow follows a form, even if they are as far apart as Hu and Yue.
The resulting consequences of good and evil cannot be divergent.
I only pray that the great assembly will awaken to impermanence and diligently cultivate meritorious deeds to sustain yourselves.
"Do not give rise to indolence and fail to exert effort," the wise have always lamented.
Even if one were to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires for ten million billion years, [it would still be insufficient].
In the end, one cannot escape the suffering of the three evil realms;
how much less can I, who have not even reached half of a hundred-year lifespan?
Within such a brief period, how could I afford to be complacent with myself?
Moreover, the delusions of the world ultimately end in decay;
that which is eternal comes to an end, and that which is high must fall.
There is separation from all that is joined, and birth must inevitably lead to death.
Who can escape high office and generous emoluments?
One's parents, brothers, and six kinds of kinsmen and relatives love one to the marrow of one's bones;
yet when the time comes to relinquish one's life, they cannot take one's place.
Prosperity, glory, nobility,
wealth, and precious treasures likewise cannot prolong the lifespan of a person.
Furthermore, one cannot seek to escape this through words, food, or drink; for who can detain that which is formless and beyond response?
As the Sūtra says:
"Death is the end."
The vital breath ceases and the spirit departs;
the physical frame becomes withered and desolate.
Within the single realm of beings, there is none that does not end in death.
At the time of casting off one's life, one undergoes great suffering and affliction;
surrounded by six kinds of kinsmen, both internal and external, they wail and weep.
The deceased is filled with panic and knows no refuge; the body is cast into emptiness as the cold breath is about to cease.
One perceives the signs of the retribution for previously performed good and evil deeds:
those who have cultivated goodness are protected by celestial deities,
while those who have committed evil have ox-headed demons at their side.
The rākṣasa wardens of hell show no mercy whatsoever;
compassionate parents and filial children cannot save one another;
and the affection between husband and wife comes to an end as they gaze upon each other.
The suffering of the body being dismembered by the wind-swords is beyond description.
At that time, the liver and gallbladder of the dying person split apart inch by inch,
and immeasurable pains and afflictions converge all at once.

The divine consciousness is frantic, as if mad or intoxicated; though it desperately wishes to give rise to a single thought of goodness or perform even a hair’s breadth of merit, it cannot do so because resentment remains in the heart.
Such suffering and distress can be borne by no one else.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When one dies, one is in a perilous place without provisions;
the destination is far distant and there is no companion."
Day and night they constantly travel without end;
it is profound and dark, devoid of light.
Having entered this place of no obstruction, one reaches a point from which there is no escape.
Having failed to cultivate merit while alive, one returns to a place of suffering at death;
its grief, poison, and bitterness cannot be cured.
This is not merely a matter of an ugly appearance that strikes fear into people, but is what the assembly of fellow practitioners here today at this site of enlightenment has come to witness.
The retributive fruits of birth and death are like a circle without end;
solitary spirits depart alone, unseen by anyone,
and cannot be sought out.
Do not entrust your affairs to material things;
rather, each of you must strive with diligence to endure toil and hardship,
and zealously cultivate the four immeasurables and the six pāramitās.
Consider that you alone must travel through the various realms of existence;
do not take comfort in your own strength and health.
You should each, with utmost sincerity, feel a sense of urgency as one and the same.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, I take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father of the World.

For those who have labored and exerted their strength in worshiping the Buddha, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this day’s site of practice now once again with utmost sincerity prostrates themselves,
casting their five limbs to the ground, and gives rise to a heart of compassion.
Without thoughts of enmity or kinship, may they act as those who,
for the sake of future rebirths, perform labor, assist with the construction of works, and provide the strength and effort to cultivate merit;

may they, along with their respective retinues, likewise serve as those who, in this very life, provide relief from the causes of suffering such as prisons, calamities, afflictions, confinement in gaols, and various punishments.
Reflecting upon their existence in the world,
although they have obtained a human body, pleasure is scarce and suffering is abundant;
shackles and fetters have never left their bodies.
By what cause is it that one either commits evil in this present life,
or is pursued by past deeds,
or finds no way to personally declare oneself free from such obligations?
Those who have committed grave offenses and face death with no protection—
may such sentient beings, each together with their retinues,
including [Name] and others, today, through a heart of compassion, [be saved].

Furthermore, I pray that all those in the prisons and penal colonies of the East and West, including those bound and confined as common criminals, those beset by calamity and hardship, and all who are afflicted by illness and lack of autonomy, [may likewise find liberation].
Together with their respective retinues,

Having utterly severed the causes of evil karma,

their lifespan is infinite and their power of wisdom is inexhaustible.
Body and mind enjoy perpetual bliss as in the third dhyāna;
they remember the suffering of the prison and keep in mind the grace of the Buddhas.
Reforming evil and cultivating goodness,
they all resolve upon the Mahāyāna,
practicing the bodhisattva path until reaching the adamantine limit (vajra-koṭi).
Furthermore, one should deliver all sentient beings,
ascending together with them to Right Enlightenment; having performed a single prostration through the sovereign power of spiritual transformations,
and having completed the confession and the arousal of the bodhicitta, one should next perform the dedication of merit.
3. Dedication of Merit. Third, the assembly of fellow practitioners at this present site of practice has already attained the resolve for enlightenment and completed what was to be accomplished.
Next, one must further dedicate each of these prior merits.
Why is this so? It is because all sentient beings are unable to attain liberation due to their attachment to worldly retributions, which they are unable to relinquish.
If one can dedicate even a fragment of merit or a hair’s breadth of goodness, one will no longer give rise to attachment toward the karmic fruit;
thus, one attains liberation, dwelling in ease and self-mastery.
Therefore, the sutras praise the practice of dedication as being of great benefit.
For this reason, on this day you should generate the mind of dedication while simultaneously exhorting all beings not to cling to karmic rewards.
We should first, with a sincere heart, prostrate ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground and take refuge,
paying homage to the Great Compassionate Father of the World.
Namo Maitreya Buddha!

The Bodhisattva’s Method of Dedication. Regarding the Bodhisattva’s Method of Dedication:
today, the great assembly of fellow practitioners at this altar have together already mastered the endurance of toil and the patience toward suffering. They have cultivated...

Act as a great relinquishment to cause the extinction of the aggregates of suffering;

Regarding these dharmas,
for the sake of both enemies and kin, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness equally to them.
All sentient beings are equal and without distinction.
Entering into the contemplation of equality, one harbors no thoughts of enmity or intimacy,
always regarding all sentient beings with eyes of love.
If sentient beings harbor resentment toward a bodhisattva and give rise to thoughts of malice or rebellion,
the bodhisattva acts as a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
skillfully taming their minds and preaching the profound Dharma for them.
Just as the great ocean cannot be destroyed by any poisons,
so too it is with the bodhisattva;
even those who are foolish, lacking wisdom, and ignorant of how to repay kindness [cannot harm them].
In this way, although sentient beings may give rise to immeasurable evils, they cannot disturb or agitate the bodhisattva’s resolve for enlightenment.
It is like the bright sun that shines universally upon all sentient beings; it does not conceal its radiance simply because there are those who lack eyesight.
The bodhisattva’s mind of the Way is also like this:
it does not become discouraged or sink because of evil,
nor does it abandon its roots of goodness because sentient beings are difficult to subdue.
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with pure faith in all roots of goodness, nurtures great compassion;
by means of these roots of goodness, they universally dedicate them to all sentient beings with a profound mind.
It is not merely a matter of verbal expression;
toward all sentient beings, they give rise to a heart of joy and a heart of clarity and purity.
A supple mind;
a mind of compassion;

A mind of gathering,

One does not see the colors of black, yellow, red, or purple that delude people;
